unit: Module 1: Development of practical skills in geology
outcome: Use geochronological principles in the field to place events in relative time order.
Define minerals as naturally occurring elements and inorganic compounds with a chemical formula, such as sulfur, copper, calcite, quartz, pyrite and galena.
Describe silicate minerals as silicon-oxygen tetrahedra forming isolated units, chains, sheets and frameworks.
Use diagnostic properties (colour, lustre, streak, cleavage, density, hardness, acid reaction) to identify and classify minerals in samples, photographs and thin sections.
Measure mineral density and hardness practically.
Classify rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic in relation to temperature and pressure in the rock cycle.
Classify igneous rocks by composition (silicic, intermediate, mafic, ultramafic) and crystal grain size, and identify them in samples and thin sections.
Use igneous textures and crystal shape as evidence of depth of formation and cooling rate.
Draw and annotate igneous textures, and describe how temperature is measured.
Explain weathering and erosion processes producing clastic material, clays, evaporites and carbonate sediment.
Explain how erosion affects the characteristics of modern sediments, including transport, the Hjulstrom curve and maturity, and carry out sieve analysis.
Recognise and measure grain sizes, including the phi scale qualitatively.
Classify siliciclastic rocks by colour, composition, grain size, shape and sorting, such as orthoquartzite, arkose and greywacke.
Classify carbonate rocks by the Dunham scheme.
Describe diagenesis and lithification: compaction, pressure dissolution, recrystallisation and cementation.
Explain how diagenesis changes porosity and permeability.
Describe metamorphism as a solid-state isochemical process: contact, dynamic and regional.
Use mineralogy and fabric to infer the parent rock, such as metaquartzite, marble, slate, phyllite, schist and gneiss.
Explain metamorphic grade and index minerals as indicators of metamorphic conditions.
Describe fossils as preserved remains or traces of organisms, including replacement and trace fossils.
Assess the reliability of the fossil record, including taphonomy, life and death assemblages and preservation potential.
Use trace fossils to infer organism behaviour and palaeoenvironment.
Use body fossils to infer behaviour and palaeoenvironment.
Use radioactive decay rates of radionuclides in minerals to give numerical ages, and plot and interpret half-life curves.
Divide the Phanerozoic into eras and periods using a biostratigraphic time sequence, recognising main invertebrate groups and the Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic faunas.
Describe the layered structure of the Earth defined by the rheological properties of the layers.
Explain how P and S wave velocities and shadow zones give indirect evidence for layers, including the state of the core.
Describe the lithosphere as a rigid, brittle layer of crust and upper mantle divided into plates.
Use gravity anomalies and isostasy as evidence for lithosphere and asthenosphere behaviour.
Use electromagnetic surveys at mid-ocean ridges to identify the lithosphere and asthenosphere.
Describe the asthenosphere as a plastic layer with 1-5% partial melting and its role in plate tectonics.
Use density of the whole Earth and surface rocks to infer core and mantle density.
Explain the geodynamo origin of the magnetic field as evidence for core subdivision.
Describe the bulk composition of the Earth inferred from meteorites (chondrites) and the Sun.
Explain the nebular hypothesis for formation of the solar system and the Earth.
Describe geothermal energy sources: heat of formation, differentiation, core formation, bombardment and radioactive decay.
Classify elements using the Goldschmidt groups: lithophile, siderophile, chalcophile and atmophile.
Explain differentiation of the Earth by partitioning of Goldschmidt groups between crust, mantle, core, atmosphere and hydrosphere.
Describe the geochemical layered structure of the Earth and the direct evidence for it.
Explain transfer of energy from within the Earth, including geothermal gradient, convection, conduction and advection.
Use earthquake seismology and seismic tomography as evidence for lithospheric plates and mantle structure.
Interpret seismograms, including finding an epicentre and shadow zones.
Describe plates as having aseismic interiors and boundaries defined by seismic activity.
Use the distribution of same-age geological features to reconstruct plate movement.
Describe evidence for mantle plumes.
Explain how GPS measurements show current relative plate movement.

subtopic: Plate driving forces and history of the theory
outcome: Explain subduction zones, plates and mantle plumes as the active limbs of convection cells.

subtopic: Plate driving forces and history of the theory
outcome: Explain ridge push at mid-ocean ridges and seafloor spreading.

subtopic: Plate driving forces and history of the theory
outcome: Compare slab pull and ridge push as drivers of plate motion.

subtopic: Plate driving forces and history of the theory
outcome: Explain how the plate tectonic paradigm emerged from earlier models and interpret developing models.
Explain mafic magma generation by partial melting at divergent boundaries and hot spots.
Explain generation of intermediate and silicic magmas at convergent boundaries.
Explain processes of intrusion and effects on country rock.
Describe major and minor intrusive bodies and use geodetic and geophysical data to detect intrusion.
Explain how changes in magma properties alter buoyancy and cause eruptions, with practical models.
Describe the characteristics of dykes, sills and lava flows.
Explain how lava composition and temperature control viscosity and volatile exsolution.
Explain how erupted material controls volcanic landforms, explosive and effusive.
Describe volcanic hazards related to magma composition, including interpreting isopachyte maps.
Describe structures from tectonic stress (bedding, faults and folds), and identify, measure and describe them on photographs, maps, cross-sections and in the field.
Construct geological cross-sections from maps and use a compass-clinometer.
Explain how stress and strain vary with temperature, confining pressure and time giving plastic or brittle deformation.
Explain how compression forms slaty cleavage.
Explain earthquakes by elastic rebound theory.
Explain shear-dominated deformation at transform boundaries.
Explain compressive deformation at convergent boundaries: fold mountains, nappes and thrusts.
Explain tensional deformation at divergent boundaries: grabens, horsts and oceanic core complexes.
Use field evidence, photographs and maps to recognise the rock cycle, including angular unconformities.
Explain how uniformitarianism and the rock cycle model developed, including catastrophism and mass extinctions.
Explain facies associations and how uniformitarianism is applied to facies by analogy with modern sediments.
Relate facies characteristics to sediment transport by wind, glaciers, rivers and shallow seas.
Identify diagnostic sedimentary structures and use them to find way-up and environment.
Construct and interpret graphic logs of modern and ancient sediments.
Describe fluvial deposition in meandering and braided rivers and alluvial fans.
Describe hot desert deposition: wadis, dunes and playa lakes.
Describe deposition in shallow siliciclastic seas.
Describe deposition in shallow carbonate seas, in, on and outside reefs.
Describe deep-water carbonate deposition above the carbonate compensation depth, including chalk and chert formation.
Apply principles of superposition, original horizontality, way-up, cross-cutting, included fragments and unconformities to interpret geological history.
Apply lithostratigraphic correlation, including lateral variation and diachronous beds.
Explain the application and limitations of relative dating.
Apply biostratigraphic correlation using zone fossils, stratigraphic range, extinction and assemblages.
Explain infrequent or hard-to-observe sedimentary processes with scientific principles: Stokes' law, bedforms, flow velocity and grain size, flocculation, and the phi scale.
Model sedimentation practically, including graded bedding, ripples and delta mouth switching.
Explain turbidity currents and the Bouma turbidite model.
Explain simple and complex deltaic models, including cyclothems.
Apply Walther's law to relate vertical sequences to lateral facies changes.
Explain deposition of banded iron-formations under Palaeoproterozoic atmosphere and ocean chemistry.
Explain how porosity controls fluid storage and permeability controls fluid movement in rocks.
Apply Darcy's law to model fluid flow, including hydrostatic pressure and hydraulic gradient.
Explain controls on groundwater quality: geochemistry, aquifer filtration and residence time.
Describe subsurface geology controlling groundwater flow: aquifers, aquicludes, water table and recharge zones.
Explain element substitution in minerals as magma cools, using solid solution series and Bowen's reaction series.
Interpret binary phase diagrams for continuous and discontinuous crystallisation.
Explain assimilation, differentiation and fractionation changing magma composition.
Explain formation of layered intrusions and metal ores by magmatic differentiation.
Relate spreading rate to seabed morphology and calculate spreading rates and radiometric ages.
Describe evidence for the structure of mid-ocean ridges from ophiolites and geophysical surveys.
Explain formation of oceanic crust and seafloor spreading at fast and slow ridges.
Explain hydrothermal processes forming massive sulfide ores.
Use metamorphic grade, index minerals and facies to reconstruct conditions and parent rock, and interpret isograds.
Explain metamorphic fabrics formed by directed stress during orogeny, and identify them in samples and thin sections.
Explain how parent rock composition and deformation conditions control the nature of rock deformation.
Explain low crustal abundances of metals and concentration factors producing ore deposits.
Explain secondary enrichment of copper ore.
Explain concentration of ore in placer deposits.
Describe geophysical and geochemical exploration methods for metals.
Explain how data sets and surveys are integrated in prospecting and estimating reserves.
Explain principles, economics and sustainability of surface and underground mining.
Explain mineral processing: leaching, crushing, tailings, froth flotation and smelting.
Explain causes and management of contaminated minewater.
Explain geological controls on reusing former mines to store waste.
Explain factors affecting earthquake impact: attenuation, moment magnitude and the Mercalli scale.
Explain how seismic energy interacts with bedrock and soil, and with groundwater (liquefaction).
Explain how civil engineering reduces seismic impacts.
Evaluate seismic hazard risk analysis and its communication to non-specialists.
Evaluate probabilistic forecasting, including calculating probability and return periods.
Evaluate deterministic predictions, such as seismic gap theory, eruption predictors and tsunami warnings.
Use GIS to synthesise geological data for disaster planning.
Explain shrinking and swelling clays, their effects and engineering mitigation.
Explain causes and effects of subsidence and its mitigation.
Explain causes and effects of landslides and slope stabilisation.
Describe the geological evidence for significant tsunamis, such as the Storegga Slide, and future risk.
Explain how interlocking and cementation affect rock strength, and how strength is measured under compression and shear.
Explain how weathering, fractures and structures change strength.
Explain how hydrostatic (pore water) pressure changes strength.
Explain how existing data and ground investigations form a geotechnical site assessment.
Explain engineering geology in tunnelling and monitoring its impacts.
Explain engineering geology in building dams and mitigating hydrogeological, slope and seismic impacts.
Explain geological understanding in remediating contaminated land and groundwater, including phytoremediation and stabilisation.
Explain Earth changes through the Phanerozoic: continent distribution, climate and atmosphere, and sea level, including the Wilson cycle and mass extinctions.
Interpret long-term changes from the geological record and geochemistry, including isotope studies and Vail sea level curves.
Relate the current rate of environmental and biological change to the evidence for an Anthropocene epoch.
Explain how trilobite morphology adapted to multiple marine niches in the Palaeozoic.
Use modern reef coral ecology to interpret tabulate and rugose fossil corals as reef indicators.
Explain brachiopod adaptation to high- and low-energy environments, and compare brachiopods with bivalves.
Explain how amphibians evolved from marine animals in the Devonian and adapted to land in the Carboniferous.
Describe the amniotic egg and its evolutionary advantage on land.
Explain dinosaur adaptation to terrestrial niches: saurischians (sauropods, theropods) and ornithischians.
Explain how birds evolved from theropods and compare birds with pterosaurs.
Describe fossil evidence for mass extinctions and their probable causes: Permo-Triassic, Ordovician-Silurian and Cretaceous-Tertiary.
Explain how mass extinctions replaced dominant forms in major habitats.
Explain the settings and conditions preserving organisms in the Burgess Shale and Chengjiang Formation, including hard and soft tissue preservation and the Cambrian explosion.
Explain the setting and conditions of exceptional preservation in the Solnhofen Limestone, including feathers and Archaeopteryx.
Apply basin analysis to North Sea hydrocarbons: settings, source, reservoir and caprocks, and maturation.
Explain migration of oil and gas, rifting and trap formation, and accumulation and loss.
Describe geophysical exploration, drilling and downhole logging, and microfossils used to locate hydrocarbons.
Apply the same principles to onshore basins, including directional drilling and fracking.
Integrate sedimentology and palaeontology of the Welsh Basin, determine palaeoenvironments by facies, and zone it with trilobites, corals and graptolites.
Apply basin analysis to UK Jurassic rocks: cyclical sedimentation, facies, trace fossils, and zonation using ammonites and belemnites.
Integrate field geology and secondary data such as maps, seismic data, well logs and fossils to understand a basin's history.
